arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Russell argued that the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act does not allow ignorance of the law as a defense.
Mr. Coakley stated that the text of the statute is the starting point for discerning congressional intent.
Chief Justice Roberts questioned the function of the bona fide error clause if intentional is read broadly.
Justice Scalia focused on the definition of the word intentional as the central issue in the case.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the scope of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. the side that brought the case argues the law bans all violations, including honest mistakes. the opposing side argues the law targets only intentional misconduct. The Court must define the term intentional in this context.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to hold that any violation of the Act is actionable, regardless of the collector's intent.
the opposing side wants the Court to hold that the Act requires proof of intentional misconduct, excluding good-faith errors.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The outcome defines the standard for civil liability under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. It determines whether debt collectors face strict liability for legal errors. It shapes the risk profile for legal professionals advising clients on debt collection. It clarifies the boundary between permissible legal interpretation and actionable misconduct.
